events.text: Alexander Graham Bell is granted the first US patent for the telephone
The first commercial telephone service across the Atlantic Ocean opens
Martin Cooper makes the first public call from a handheld mobile phone in Manhattan
Samuel Morse opens his Washington to Baltimore telegraph line with 'What hath God wrought'

reveal.explanation: Morse's dots and dashes ran between Washington and Baltimore a generation before Bell's patent put a human voice on the wire. Half a century after that, voices were crossing the Atlantic by radio, and by 1973 a phone could be carried in the hand.

sources.excerpt: On May 24, 1844, the line was officially opened as Morse sent the now-famous words, "What hath God wrought," from the Supreme Court chamber in the basement of the U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., to the B&O's Mount Clare Station in Baltimore.
On March 7, 1876, the U.S. Patent Office issued Bell patent 174,465.
On January 7, 1927, W. S. Gifford, president of the American Telephone & Telegraph Company, called Evelyn P. Murray to test the first commercial telephone line across the Atlantic Ocean.
On April 3, 1973, Cooper placed the first public call from a handheld portable cell phone while working at Motorola, from a Manhattan sidewalk to his counterpart at competitor Bell Labs.

editorNotes: Alternatives checked: Bell's patent was filed on 14 February 1876 and issued on 7 March 1876, the same year; Morse's line was demonstrated on 1 May 1844 and officially opened on 24 May 1844; the 1927 transatlantic service was carried by radio, and the first telephone cable did not follow until 1956, so the event text says service rather than cable; Cooper's DynaTAC did not reach the market until 1983, so the text names the call rather than the phone's sale.
